industry: Oil and Gas Exploration and Production
cause: Falls from height
narrative:
On an offshore drilling rig, on 1 September 2025, personnel and marine crew were installing handrails on top of a 
unit on the main deck. Handrail sections (60–90 kg) were lifted by deck crane to the top of the unit, where an operator 
worked at height to receive and install them, using fall-arrest equipment. The operator initially attached his lanyard 
to the stairs, then to handrail, and later to another section to reach the final corner section. To fit the last section, he 
had to lift and adjust some of the handrail. The locking pins were weakly retained and the chain/carabiner secondary 
securing arrangement did not prevent them from sliding out. The section of the handrail tilted and fell, pulling the 
operator with it. He fell approximately 4.3 m to deck, landing partly on the fallen handrail. The incident resulted in an 
LTI and a dropped object with calculated energy of 2733 J, with assessed potential for a single fatality.
what_went_wrong:
The units were not designed to support safe work at height: the only structurally adequate anchoring points (lifting 
eyes) were located below top deck level and were occupied by lifting bridles during installation, leaving no suitable 
anchor points available. The operator therefore clipped his fall-arrest lanyard to a handrail section that was only 
temporarily secured by a pin, chain, and carabiner. The handrail securing design was inherently weak; on the short 
side of the container, the locking pin had only ~2 mm mechanical engagement and could easily slide out, and the 
chain/carabiner arrangement offered a false sense of security. The installation and commissioning procedure 
mentioned work at height and scaffolding, but did not clearly explain how the handrails should be installed or 
secured, nor the purpose or requirement for scaffold. No scaffold was erected, and the crew changed the intended 
installation sequence, requiring lifting and moving the section used as an anchor. Competence requirements for 
work at height (Norog 113) were not formalised in the competence matrix; several involved personnel lacked formal 
practical WAH training and were unaware of approved anchor point requirements. Project planning and follow-up 
from onshore were insufficient, and the contractor equipment checklist process was not effectively applied.
corrective_actions:
Work at height must never rely on temporary structures (such as partially installed handrails) as anchoring points. 
Units that require routine or installation work at height must be designed with suitable, certified anchor points, or 
work must be carried out from properly designed scaffolding or other engineered access solutions. Competence 
requirements for working at height (incl. practical training and anchor-point assessment) must be explicitly built 
into contractor competence matrices and verified before mobilisation. Installation and commissioning procedures 
for vendor packages must clearly describe safe installation methods, including detailed handrail installation 
sequences, locking mechanisms, and when scaffolding is mandatory. Work permits that bundle many high-
risk activities can obscure critical controls; large scopes should be broken into smaller work procedures where 
necessary to ensure hazards and controls are fully understood. A robust equipment and project-follow-up process 
is needed, including use of the correct contractor equipment checklist and clear assignment of onshore and 
offshore responsibility for installation planning and oversight.

industry: Oil and Gas Production and Operations
narrative:
During a planned maintenance activity to replace fasteners on a gas injection pipeline, a high-pressure release of a 
flammable gas mixture occurred. The release happened as the maintenance crew attempted to perform a sequence 
of ‘hot bolting,’ a procedure involving the removal and replacement of bolts on a flange while the pipeline remained 
pressurized. Due to failures in procedural adherence and execution, the flange opened unexpectedly, resulting in a 
jet of cold, pressurized gas that struck workers, causing eye injuries and requiring urgent medical evacuation.
what_went_wrong:
The immediate cause of the incident was the inability to maintain the minimum torque required for flange tightness. 
Critical errors included the use of incorrect tools, performing the task in an improper sequence, and a lack of 
adequate qualification among those involved. Procedures lacked clear guidance on risk assessment and practical 
execution, with insufficient focus on detailed planning and inspection prior to the task. Administrative safeguards 
failed, particularly in terms of controlling the tools used and ensuring workers possessed the specific technical 
competence demanded by both the process and normative standards. While layered protections such as emergency 
shutdown and gas detection responded effectively to limit escalation, preventive measures did not.
corrective_actions:
This event underscored that high-criticality tasks like hot bolting demand strict compliance with technical 
standards, practical procedures that are clearly defined and executable, and that relying solely on administrative 
controls is inadequate. The organization must ensure that risk assessments and planning encompass real 
working conditions and that exposure to hazardous situations is controlled by robust physical, engineering, and 
organizational safeguards rather than individual choices.
Main recommendations derived from the event were:
Revise technical standards for hot bolting to ensure that all engineering risk assessment items are addressed 
during planning, documented and implemented in execution.
Update procedures so they fully comply with all normative requirements, and reinforce the need for strict adherence 
in execution—as deviations may lead to uncontrolled loss of containment.
Adapt the permit to work system to explicitly prohibit unsuitable tools (such as hammers) for hot bolting, 
incorporating regulatory restrictions.
Improve hot bolting services by specifying professional qualifications required, and revise contract requirements to 
ensure only appropriately trained personnel are assigned to such critical tasks.
Increase the categorization of permits for hot bolting, demanding more rigorous analysis during planning.

specifications for the thermal isolator.

includes defined replacement criteria and condition assessments based on operational exposure, rather than time-

cause: Explosion, fire or burns
narrative:
On 27 December at approximately 07:30, cleaning cloths contaminated with cooking oil were washed and dried in 
the laundry.
After drying, the cloths were placed on the floor inside an open bag next to other cloths. Later, all laundry 
ventilation, exhaust, and air-conditioning systems were switched off while the room was unattended.
At approximately 13:15, the cloths began releasing smoke and an incipient fire developed. The steward used a dry 
chemical extinguisher and the fire brigade extinguished the fire.
No injuries or damage occurred, but the event had serious fire potential.
what_went_wrong:
• Oil-contaminated cloths were washed and dried without special handling precautions.
• Hot cloths were stored in a pile/bag, allowing heat accumulation and self-heating.
• Laundry ventilation and cooling were shut down while the cloths were unattended.
• No procedure existed for segregation, cooling, or disposal of oily rags.
• Hazard of spontaneous combustion from oil-soaked rags was not recognised.
corrective_actions:
• Segregate oil/grease contaminated cloths before laundering.
• Do not place recently dried cloths in piles, bags, or enclosed areas - allow them to cool individually in a 
ventilated metal container or spread out.
• Maintain ventilation/exhaust until materials have cooled.
• Implement procedures for handling and disposal of contaminated rags.
• Train personnel on spontaneous combustion risks (oils, hydrocarbons, solvents).
• Provide fire-resistant rag bins and designated storage areas.

cause: Dropped objects
narrative:
During a heavy rainstorm, two aluminium composite panels (component of the external cladding material for the 
Office building) dislodged and dropped. The two (2) panels, each weighing 9.8kgs and measuring 1.11x1.49ms, 
dropped from about a height of 22.35 meters. The fallen panels were found Infront of the South Wing Power room, 
and the affected area was promptly cordoned off to prevent further hazards. Additionally, multiple panels were 
observed hanging loosely, posing a potential safety risk to occupants and visitors.
what_went_wrong:
1. Aluminium composite panels not airtight. - Previous investigations revealed that no consideration was given 
to the potential for panels falling during design and installation. Furthermore, subsequent structural integrity 
assessments did not clearly establish the mode of failure and effective mitigation measures to prevent recurrence.
Additionally, in cases where potentially falling aluminium composite panels have been reported, remedial actions to 
remove and reinstall such panels are not promptly executed, despite the high potential impact of a dropped panel.
2. Corrective action process not effectively implemented. - There has been recurring near misses involving dropped 
Aluminium Composite Panels in 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2024. However, corrective actions, such as implementing 
monthly and quarterly drop inspections, have not been sustained.
Furthermore, planned preventive maintenance and other assurance activities that were instituted have not been 
consistently followed and remain areas requiring improvement. For instance, the annual integrity assessment for 
2023 and 2024 were not conducted as planned.
corrective_actions:
1. Conduct an integrity inspection and assessment of the external of the entire building to identify any areas of loose 
cladding and fix them immediately to prevent any potential recurrence of the incident in the short term.
2. Re-institute the conduct of the annual inspection programme of the entire exterior of the building's facade to 
identify any areas of loose cladding and fix them immediately to prevent any potential dropped objects.

surfaces.

cause: Struck by (not dropped object)
narrative:
While parking the starboard (STBD) crane following routine lifting operations, the crane boom was brought down 
into the boom rest abruptly rather than in a controlled manner. This sudden placement generated an unexpected 
impact load on the crane structure, producing a loud bang that was heard in the vicinity of the crane pedestal and 
surrounding areas.
The abrupt motion and resulting impact load may have introduced a shock event into the crane’s hydraulic or 
electrical systems. A process shutdown occurred minutes after this impact, and although the causal link has not yet 
been fully established, the timing suggests the crane event may have contributed to or triggered the shutdown.
what_went_wrong:
• Crane boom impacted boom rest heavily.
• Crane incorrectly lowered at the boom rest.
• Lack of experience of Crane Operator.
corrective_actions:
1. Mandatory contractor equipment specific training familiarization to be performed onboard and documented with 
new crane operators.
2. Selection of candidates for temporary cover to be formalized with the minimum experience requirement for 
contractor operations
3. New crane operators to be mobilized in advance to come offshore and undergo supervision monitored by the 
facility crane operator for a defined supervision period.
4. Non-destructive testing to be performed at the crane's boom & cradle by 3rd party.

what_went_wrong:

The impact indicates a loss of control of stored mechanical energy or unexpected movement/ejection of a 
component during valve-related activities.
Critical hazards associated with heavy components and pressurized systems were not effectively controlled at the

corrective_actions:
Valve interventions on large-diameter systems are high-risk activities and require strict control of stored energy 
(pressure, mechanical, gravitational).
Full isolation, depressurization, verification of zero energy, and mechanical securing of components must be 
completed before any work begins.
Exclusion zones and line-of-fire controls are mandatory when working with heavy or potentially mobile metallic 
components.
Trainees must not be exposed to critical tasks without direct supervision, clear role definition, and confirmation of 
competency.
Permit to Work (PTW), Job Safety Analysis (JSA), and LOTO procedures must explicitly address:
• Component movement or ejection.
• Required restraints and tooling.
• Safe positioning of personnel.
Contractor safety management must ensure alignment with site standards, including training, supervision, and 
enforcement of stop-work authority.
Fatal events reinforce that engineering and procedural controls must never rely solely on experience or 
assumptions; verification is essential.

narrative:
An incident occurred at NGL Loading Bay involving the overfilling of a truck and subsequent spill of NGL. The event 
resulted from the failure of the High-High level switch, which did not initiate the automatic system shutdown as 
designed. The abnormal condition was identified through CCTV monitoring, which revealed the product overflow. 
Immediate intervention was undertaken by activating the emergency shutdown push button, thereby halting loading 
operations.
what_went_wrong:
1. Failure of Primary Level Control Barrier - high-high level switch failed to operate and did not initiate the 
automatic closure of the associated loading valves.
2. Design Flaws in Timer-Based Overfill Protection - The tertiary overfill protection relied on a preset loading timer 
based on a fixed batch concept, which did not account for varying tanker sizes or flow rates. 
3. Degraded Condition of Critical Equipment - The level switch assembly and cabling were found to be frequently 
damaged due to poor ergonomic design of the vapor extraction and switch mounting arrangements, and 
mechanical interference during tanker installation and removal.

4. Redundant Barrier Not Maintained in Practice - A local high-level switch, previously identified as a safety barrier 
in earlier designs and referenced in the Control and Operating Philosophy, was retained physically but removed as a 
functional barrier during the re-HAZOP. 
5. Procedural and Human Factors Weaknesses - Although pre-loading checks are required, they did not adequately 
account for the degraded condition of key safeguards.
The dependency on a single barrier and the lack of operator awareness about available fallback systems further 
compounded the risk.
corrective_actions:
1. Remove the logic for the end of sequence timer protection and remove its reference from the Control and 
Philosophy procedure. 
2. Carry out an ergonomic design assessment of the Hatch Cover assembly
3. Incorporate the local high-level Alarm as the secondary barrier.
4. Conduct a comprehensive Safety Critical Task Analysis’s (SCTA) of the NGL road tanker loading operation. 
5. Develop detailed Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) for the NGL/LPG and
tanker loading process.
6. Deliver a training program to all affected stakeholders.

industry: Oil and Gas Production and Operations
narrative:
On March 7th, 2025, the platform experienced a major process safety incident when the hinge pin of the dome 
on a Cargo Tank starboard catastrophically failed. The rupture of the hinge pin resulted in the complete loss of 
mechanical restraint of the dome, causing the dome cover to fully open and exposing the entire tank opening to 
atmosphere. This structural failure led to the uncontrolled release of a flammable gas mixture directly onto the deck.
The plant’s gas detection system was activated, initiating an emergency shutdown (ESD). Personnel were mustered 
in the accommodation module; however, a continuous flammable gas cloud was extending laterally across the full 
width of the platform, spanning from one side to the other. As a result, access to the muster location necessarily 
required personnel to pass through the flammable gas cloud.
The tanks were depressurized both through the fully open dome, which was already providing an unrestricted 
release path, and by remotely opening the vent stacks. Despite these depressurization measures, the uncontrolled 
release continued for nearly one hour, until the tanks were fully vented and pressure equalized with the atmosphere.
Fortunately, there were no injuries, fires, explosions, or environmental impacts. Nevertheless, production was 
halted, and personnel were exposed to significant risk due to the prolonged presence of a flammable atmosphere 
across the installation.
what_went_wrong:
The root cause investigation identified that the main threat was progressive corrosion on the dome’s hinge pin, 
caused by an inadequate weld that was smaller than specified in the original design. Weaknesses in the preventive 
safety barriers allowed this defect to persist: the inspection plan did not require detailed checks on the dome pin, 
and a maintenance anomaly had been incorrectly reported in the system (as a generic defect note instead of a 
specific inspection note, and linked to a general location instead of the dome pin). These failures in inspection and 
anomaly management meant the integrity problem was neither prioritized nor properly addressed, allowing the 
degradation to continue unnoticed until catastrophic failure.
corrective_actions:
The incident highlighted the need for robust inspection and maintenance protocols focused on critical structural 
joints of tank covers. Inspections must be properly planned and rigorously executed to verify weld quality, 
dimensional compliance, and integrity at hinge assemblies, pivot points, and attachment areas. Maintenance 
reporting processes should require precise classification and direct linkage of each finding to the exact component 
affected, avoiding generic location references. Information management systems must include all relevant 
structural elements to prevent misregistration or omission of critical observations.
Design and procurement standards should mandate verification of structural joints and weld integrity at 
commissioning and throughout the operational lifecycle, incorporating these checks into routine field inspections.

Reporting procedures for structural integrity issues within asset management systems must be clearly defined 
and consistently applied, with personnel retrained to ensure correct categorization and traceability. Existing 
maintenance records related to tank cover joints should be reviewed and corrected to ensure accurate component-
level identification.
Inspection plans must require comprehensive structural assessments of tank covers, including photographic or 
equivalent documentation to ensure traceability and accountability. In addition, design standards should incorporate 
secondary locking or securing devices on tank covers and other safety-critical access points to reduce the risk of 
accidental release or structural failure.
Summary of Main Recommendations:
• Initiate targeted inspections of tank cover hinge joints to confirm weld quality and dimensional compliance.
• Revise inspection checklists to include structural joint verification during acceptance of new tank units and 
periodically thereafter.
• Clarify and enforce correct asset management reporting categories and retrain inspection and maintenance 
personnel.
• Audit existing maintenance reports on tank cover areas and correct inaccurate or generic location assignments.
• Update information systems to allow individual selection of all tank cover components when registering 
anomalies.
• Enhance inspection procedures to require detailed documentation and visual traceability of findings.
• Implement design upgrades with secondary securing devices for tank covers and other safety-critical access 
points.

narrative:
During the installation of a subsea telescopic clamp on the well shaft beneath the offshore platform, the Diving 
Service team encountered a safety-critical situation when a support vessel unexpectedly approached the platform, 
despite all established safety measures being in place. The vessel’s captain was promptly contacted and informed 
that underwater diving operations were in progress.
what_went_wrong:
• The support vessel entered the platform vicinity without maintaining the required safe distance.
• Insufficient communication with vessel captain.
• While all safety measures on the platform and by the diving team were followed, the control barrier against 
external vessel movements failed.
• Reliance on reactive communication (contacting the captain after the approach) rather than proactive control 
allowed a near-miss.
• The incident primarily resulted from lack of effective marine coordination and vessel traffic control, leading to a 
near-miss with potentially severe consequences for diving operations.
corrective_actions:
• Ensure all vessels operating near offshore platforms are aware of ongoing diving operations.
• Strengthen coordination with support vessels and vessel traffic control to enforce exclusion zones proactively.
• Establish mandatory pre-approach notifications for all vessels near the platform.
• Ensure immediate and continuous communication channels between the platform, diving team, and vessel 
captains.

cause: Dropped objects
narrative:
During offloading of a delivery of structural steel, a stacked load became unstable while the final securement strap 
was being removed. A beam fell from the trailer and struck a worker. Emergency response was initiated, the beam 
was removed from contact, and the worker was transported for medical assessment and treatment.
what_went_wrong:
The load became unstable during the unstrapping step and a beam dropped unexpectedly. Pre-job planning 
and cargo-management expectations were not consistently communicated to all parties involved in the offload, 
including the driver, and required verification steps (e.g., use of task hazard assessment / cargo management 
processes) were not effectively applied at the subcontractor interface.
corrective_actions:
Require that all personnel involved in delivery/offloading are included in the pre-job briefing and the offload plan. 
Verify load securement and offloading controls against applicable standards and site expectations before straps are 
removed, and use engineered controls (e.g., suitable bunks/deck-pin/barrier arrangements) where practicable to 
reduce reliance on procedural controls alone.

PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Protective Methods: Equipment or materials not secured

industry: Oil and Gas Exploration and Production
cause: Explosion, fire or burns
narrative:
On January 19, 2025, during restart attempts of the HP-A Gas Compressor following corrective maintenance, 
an unusually loud noise was heard from the exhaust. Seconds later, the fire alarm was triggered, and it was 
observed that the exhaust structure had fallen off. Technicians in the vicinity immediately pressed the compressor’s 
emergency stop button and evacuated the facility. Simultaneously, the emergency response team was activated, and 
the on-scene commander initiated a full facility shutdown using a manual call point near the compressor building. 
Once the source of the loud noise was confirmed to be the HP-A compressor, with the exhaust lying on the ground, 
the area was cordoned off, and an investigation was launched. The compressor was manually shut down, and the 
ESD-1 emergency stop was activated.
what_went_wrong:
During the starting of gas lift compressor (HP-A), the exhaust pipe of the engine driving the reciprocating 
compressor broke and fell off after several attempts to start it, subsequently activating the fire alarm.
corrective_actions:
The crew was not very familiar with the model of engine and didn't know how to react after 1 or 2 attempts to 
restart.
The operating manual was in English not fully understood by the maintenance team.
